name: River rock
seoDesc: River rock: work out width from the length and the depth. A free construction calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: width is what the River rock calculator works out, and it gets there from the length, the depth, the volume and the volume needed. Think of it as a shortcut for a materials order or a planning estimate you want to get roughly right first time. Nothing repaints underneath you: edit a field, press Calculate, and the new answer appears. That is how you find out which input the result is sensitive to.

sections.title: How does the River rock calculator work?
sections.html:
The River rock calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports width in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the rock type); then you type in the length, the depth, the volume and the volume needed.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• Pick the option that matches your case — 20 options, such as standard river rock, bank gravel and cheshire pink gravel. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in meters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 34 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in centimeters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 34 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in cubic meters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 40 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in cubic meters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 40 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in US Dollar. The unit chip switches it to any of the 113 supported units.

One field on this form is a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the River rock calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Width=area ÷ length
Area=volume ÷ depth
Wastage=-100 + 100 × volume needed ÷ volume
Weight needed=density × volume needed
Weight needed=total cost ÷ price per one unit of mass
Price per one unit of volume=total cost ÷ volume needed

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Density, opening in kilograms per cubic meter
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Area, opening in square meters
  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Volume, opening in cubic meters
  • %, opening in percent
  • Volume, opening in cubic meters

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The River rock calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Quoting a job where areas and quantities drive the price
  • Checking a supplier's figure against your own measurements
  • Ordering material and not wanting a second trip
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the length, the depth and the volume — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the River rock calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns width, derived from the length, the depth and the volume. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the River rock calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the length, the depth, the volume and the volume needed, which is 6 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter density in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Density opens in kilograms per cubic meter and the chip beside it offers 28 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Density = 0 kg/m³. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the River rock calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
